consensus_findings.headline: Heir location is paid on contingency, never on up-front fees.

Charging an heir an advance fee is treated as the single clearest marker of a predatory or unlicensed operator.

claims_requiring_verification.topic_title: State Fee Caps, Waiting Periods, PI Licensing & UPL Rules
claims_requiring_verification.question: Does the California 10% statutory cap on unclaimed-property recovery agreements also bind heir-finder fees in probate estate assignments?
conflicting_views: Sources treat the ~10% ceiling in California Code of Civil Procedure § 1582 as a blanket cap on every heir-finder fee charged in the state.

Other sources describe the cap as specific to agreements to recover property held by the state controller after escheat, leaving probate-court estate assignments to a reasonableness review by the probate judge.
A third group reports negotiating 15-35% on probate matters in California without objection, which only makes sense if the statutory cap is not universal.
claims_requiring_verification.editorial_resolution: Present the cap as scope-limited rather than universal: quote the statute's own description of the agreements it governs, note that probate assignments are separately subject to court approval and reasonableness review, and instruct the reader to confirm which track their file is on before quoting a percentage.

claims_requiring_verification.question: Does locating heirs for compensation require a private investigator license in Florida, Texas or Arizona?
conflicting_views: Several operators state flatly that searching for a person for pay is regulated investigative activity in these states and requires a licensed PI or an agency affiliation.
Others argue that public-record genealogy research is exempt and that the license only attaches when surveillance or investigation of a living subject's conduct is involved.
A further view is that the trigger is the business activity of locating a person for a fee, regardless of whether the research is conducted from public records.
claims_requiring_verification.editorial_resolution: Treat licensing as a threshold compliance question, not a footnote: direct the reader to the named state licensing authority, describe the fact patterns that commonly trigger review, and avoid asserting any state-specific exemption as settled.

claims_requiring_verification.topic_title: Fee Agreements, Assignments of Interest & Escrow Disbursement
claims_requiring_verification.question: Is taking an assignment of a heir's interest in an estate enforceable, or vulnerable as champerty or an unconscionable bargain?
conflicting_views: Operators report using outright assignments of interest as the cleanest way to secure payment directly from the estate.
Others warn that courts in champerty-sensitive jurisdictions have voided or reduced such assignments where the heir was uninformed of the estate's value.
A middle view holds that a percentage fee agreement with an irrevocable direction to pay from escrow survives scrutiny where a bare assignment does not.
claims_requiring_verification.editorial_resolution: Recommend the disclosure-forward structure as the default — fee agreement plus escrow direction, with the estate identified once the heir signs — and present bare assignment as a jurisdiction-specific instrument requiring local counsel.

claims_requiring_verification.question: Where is the line between permissible heir-location work and the unauthorized practice of law?

Others hold that selecting the filing, advising on entitlement, or appearing for the heir is law practice and must be routed to a licensed attorney.
A third position is that the locator may assemble and transmit evidence but must never advise the heir on legal rights or strategy.

claims_requiring_verification.question: Is the contingency percentage computed on the gross estate value or on the net amount actually distributable to the located heir?
conflicting_views: Headline case figures in the corpus are quoted against gross estate or gross property value.
Operators describing actual settlement statements compute the fee on the heir's net distributable share after debts, liens, taxes, administration costs and co-heir splits.
Some agreements are described as fixing the percentage on recovered funds received, which differs again where property is sold rather than distributed in kind.
claims_requiring_verification.editorial_resolution: Standardize on net distributable share to the specific heir as the manual's arithmetic base, show the gross-to-net waterfall explicitly, and label any gross-value figures drawn from the corpus as illustrative rather than as expected earnings.

conflicting_views.topic_title: State Fee Caps, Waiting Periods, PI Licensing & UPL Rules
conflicting_views.question: Does the California 10% statutory cap on unclaimed-property recovery agreements also bind heir-finder fees in probate estate assignments?
conflicting_views: Sources treat the ~10% ceiling in California Code of Civil Procedure § 1582 as a blanket cap on every heir-finder fee charged in the state.

Other sources describe the cap as specific to agreements to recover property held by the state controller after escheat, leaving probate-court estate assignments to a reasonableness review by the probate judge.
A third group reports negotiating 15-35% on probate matters in California without objection, which only makes sense if the statutory cap is not universal.
conflicting_views.editorial_resolution: Present the cap as scope-limited rather than universal: quote the statute's own description of the agreements it governs, note that probate assignments are separately subject to court approval and reasonableness review, and instruct the reader to confirm which track their file is on before quoting a percentage.

conflicting_views.question: Does locating heirs for compensation require a private investigator license in Florida, Texas or Arizona?
conflicting_views: Several operators state flatly that searching for a person for pay is regulated investigative activity in these states and requires a licensed PI or an agency affiliation.
Others argue that public-record genealogy research is exempt and that the license only attaches when surveillance or investigation of a living subject's conduct is involved.
A further view is that the trigger is the business activity of locating a person for a fee, regardless of whether the research is conducted from public records.
conflicting_views.editorial_resolution: Treat licensing as a threshold compliance question, not a footnote: direct the reader to the named state licensing authority, describe the fact patterns that commonly trigger review, and avoid asserting any state-specific exemption as settled.

conflicting_views.topic_title: Fee Agreements, Assignments of Interest & Escrow Disbursement
conflicting_views.question: Is taking an assignment of a heir's interest in an estate enforceable, or vulnerable as champerty or an unconscionable bargain?
conflicting_views: Operators report using outright assignments of interest as the cleanest way to secure payment directly from the estate.
Others warn that courts in champerty-sensitive jurisdictions have voided or reduced such assignments where the heir was uninformed of the estate's value.
A middle view holds that a percentage fee agreement with an irrevocable direction to pay from escrow survives scrutiny where a bare assignment does not.
conflicting_views.editorial_resolution: Recommend the disclosure-forward structure as the default — fee agreement plus escrow direction, with the estate identified once the heir signs — and present bare assignment as a jurisdiction-specific instrument requiring local counsel.

conflicting_views.question: Is the contingency percentage computed on the gross estate value or on the net amount actually distributable to the located heir?
conflicting_views: Headline case figures in the corpus are quoted against gross estate or gross property value.
Operators describing actual settlement statements compute the fee on the heir's net distributable share after debts, liens, taxes, administration costs and co-heir splits.
